issues.title: AWG Router: AmneziaWG server panel with cascade routing and load balancing
issues.body:
I maintain AWG Router, an open-source (MIT) web panel for AmneziaWG servers: https://github.com/r-slashslash/AWG-Router

**Routing.** Clients can exit through other AWG servers or SOCKS5 proxies, chosen networks go direct, rules can be set per client and per domain. Domain rules work by redirecting TCP 80/443 to a local proxy that reads SNI/Host; QUIC is blocked for those clients, and ECH sites can't be matched. Each exit has its own routing table with an `unreachable` fallback, so when an exit is down traffic is dropped, not leaked. The tunnel is IPv4-only: clients get `::/0` and IPv6 is dropped inside.

**Panel exposure.** The panel lives under a secret path; everything outside it is minimal and answers with a generic `Server` header. The browser never contacts third-party hosts.

**SOCKS5 exit health.** A local Xray answers "connected" before it has reached the far side, so the check sends a TLS ClientHello after CONNECT and requires at least one byte back.

I'd welcome feedback, especially on fingerprinting and on how this behaves on real networks in Russia, Iran and China.

issues.title: tun: end UDP flows and cancel dispatches when the inbound closes
issues.body:
## Problem

Closing a core instance that has a `tun` inbound leaves its UDP flows alive, and everything they hold with them.

- `Handler.Init` detaches the handler's context from the instance (`core.ToBackgroundDetachedContext`), and nothing cancels it on `Close`.
- `stack.Close` resets the TCP connections and closes the sockets opened by `DialUDP`, but never touches the UDP flow table (`udpConnectionHandler.udpConns`).

So each UDP flow's reader keeps waiting on its packet queue after `Close`, which pins its XUDP mux session, the mux `ClientWorker` and that worker's connection to the server.

Measured in a client that embeds the tun inbound and restarts the instance per session (goroutine origins from `runtime.Stack`): about 80 goroutines, 0.8 MB of live heap and stacks, and one established outbound connection leaked per instance, with no decay over 8+ minutes. After 25 instances: 1600 goroutines, all created by `tun.(*udpConnectionHandler).HandlePacket`, `mux.(*ClientWorker).Dispatch`, `mux.NewClientWorker` and `mux.(*DialingWorkerFactory).Create`, and 17 established connections to the server.

## Fix

- `Handler` owns a `cancel` for its detached context and calls it in `Close` before closing the stack, so in-flight dispatches unwind (also the ones not blocked on the reader).
- `stack.Close` ends every UDP flow (`udpConnectionHandler.closeAll`): their readers get EOF, the dispatches return and release their outbounds. The flow table also refuses new flows from then on, mirroring `handleTCP`'s `closed` check: a packet already in flight between the stack closing and the tun closing used to open a fresh flow (and, with a mux outbound, dial a worker) during shutdown.

The remaining XUDP mux workers then close on the mux client's idle check (two 16 s monitor ticks after their last session), after which goroutines and heap are back at the baseline and no server connections remain.

## Verification

- New tests: `TestUDPHandlerCloseAllEndsFlows` (flows end on close, a late packet opens none) and `TestHandlerCloseCancelsDispatches` (a dispatch that is not reading returns when the handler closes). `go test -race ./proxy/tun/` passes.
- With the patch, 20 instance start/stop cycles end with 0 established connections to the server and the baseline goroutine count; without it, 17 connections and 1600 goroutines that never go away.

issues.title: XDNS finalmask: `tcp://` resolvers send unframed queries; a domain like `t.example.com.` crashes the client
issues.body:
### Integrity requirements

- [x] I have read all the comments in the issue template and ensured that this issue meet the requirements.
- [x] I confirm that I have read the documentation, understand the meaning of all the configuration items I wrote, and did not pile up seemingly useful options or default values.
- [x] I provided the complete config and logs, rather than just providing the truncated parts based on my own judgment.
- [x] I searched issues and did not find any similar issues.
- [x] The problem can be successfully reproduced in the latest Release

### Description

Two bugs in the XDNS client, both from #6718. Reproduced with v26.10.31 built from the tag (a4a3dff, go1.27.3); the three files involved are unchanged on `main`.

**1. `tcp://` resolvers send DNS messages without the two-byte length prefix**

`transport/internet/finalmask/xdns/resolver_tcp.go:127`:

```go
_ = binary.Write(r.conn, binary.BigEndian, len(p))
_, _ = r.conn.Write(p)
```

`binary.Write` takes only fixed-size values. Given an `int`, it returns `binary.Write: some values are not fixed-sized in type int` and writes nothing, and the error is dropped. So each query goes out bare. A DNS server reads the random query ID as the length (RFC 1035 §4.2.2, RFC 7766 §8) and never answers. Against a `miekg/dns` TCP server, `TCPResolver` gets no reply within 5 s; a `dns.Client{Net: "tcp"}` asking the same question does get one. Reading answers (`recv`) handles the prefix correctly.

Possible fix, a single write as RFC 7766 §8 recommends:

```go
b := make([]byte, 2+len(p))
binary.BigEndian.PutUint16(b, uint16(len(p)))
copy(b[2:], p)
_, _ = r.conn.Write(b)
```

**2. A domain with an empty label, or a label over 63 bytes, passes the config check and then panics the process**

`NewDomain` (`domain.go:82`) rejects only `..` and builds the name with `dnsmessage.NewName(domain + ".")`, which checks only the total length. So `t.example.com.` (trailing dot), `a.`, `.a`, `.`, an empty name and a 64-byte label are all accepted, by `xray run -test` too. On the first packet, `client.go:152` calls `common.Must2(msg.AppendPack(buf[:0]))`. Packing fails with `zero length segment` or `segment length too long`. The panic, in mKCP's updater goroutine, makes the process exit with status 2. `Must2`'s own comment says that errors user input can cause must be handled.

`NewDomain` already computes `ascii, err := idna.ToASCII(domain)` and trims its dots, then never uses it. Building the name from `ascii` would make `t.example.com.` mean `t.example.com`. It would also fix IDN names, which now go on the wire as raw UTF-8: `тест.рф.` instead of `xn--e1aybc.xn--p1ai.`, the name the zone is delegated under. An empty result and labels over 63 bytes would still need rejecting, for example:

```go
ascii = strings.Trim(ascii, ".")
if ascii == "" {
	return nil, errors.New("empty domain")
}
for _, label := range strings.Split(ascii, ".") {
	if len(label) == 0 || len(label) > 63 {
		return nil, errors.New("invalid domain")
	}
}
name, err := dnsmessage.NewName(ascii + ".")
```

The server calls `NewDomain` too, so for IDN names both sides would change together. If `send` handled the `AppendPack` error instead of using `Must2`, a bad name would drop the packet and the process would keep running.

With both changes applied, `go test ./transport/internet/finalmask/xdns/` still passes. `TCPResolver` then gets the `miekg/dns` server's answer, and a client for `t.example.com.` sends its queries instead of panicking.

### Reproduction Method

Only the client is needed. For bug 2, nothing has to listen on 127.0.0.1:10443 or :10053: the crash comes before anything is sent.

Bug 2:

1. With the client config below, `xray run -test -c client.json` prints `Configuration OK.`
2. Run `xray run -c client.json`, then `curl --socks5 127.0.0.1:10808 http://127.0.0.1:9/`.
3. Xray exits with status 2 and the panic in the client log below. A 64-byte label (`aaaa…a.example.com`) gives `segment length too long` inst

issues.title: TUN inbound: Half-close the app connection when the outbound is done, instead of waiting for `uplinkOnly`
issues.body:
## Why

With Xray's TUN as the system VPN, an app that reads a response until the server closes waits about 1 s more than it should on every such connection. The outbound already knows the response is over, but TUN keeps the app's connection open until the whole dispatch ends, and that happens only after `uplinkOnly`. Examples are HTTP/1.0 without `Content-Length`, RTSP (Moonlight in #5845) and simple request and reply protocols. With this change the app gets the end of the response right away

## What changed

- TUN sends FIN to the app as soon as the outbound is done with the response. The app can still send, and the connection is closed as before when the dispatch is over
- the lightweight TCP stack gets `CloseWrite` for that
- the rest of the core still closes links in pairs, as agreed in the thread

## Testing and limits

- `TestTCPCloseWrite` checks that FIN goes out, that data from the app is still read after it and that `Close` sends nothing more. `go test -race ./proxy/tun` passes
- this helps only when the outbound itself sees the end of the response, for example freedom or VMess. Over VLESS the outbound ends only after `uplinkOnly` on the server, so the wait there stays

Related #5845 #7345

issues.body:
### Integrity requirements

- [X] I have read all the comments in the issue template and ensured that this issue meet the requirements.
- [X] I confirm that I have read the documentation, understand the meaning of all the configuration items I wrote, and did not pile up seemingly useful options or default values.
- [X] I provided the complete config and logs, rather than just providing the truncated parts based on my own judgment.
- [X] I searched issues and did not find any similar issues.
- [X] The problem can be successfully reproduced in the latest Release

### Description

> 简述：在 v26.10.17（与 main 相同）中，如果 XDRIVE 客户端在下载中途消失（进程被杀或断网），服务端无法察觉：它会继续从目标读取，并把剩余的整个响应写入存储（复现中 20 秒内写入约 235 MiB、607 个对象）。这些对象要等服务端的 mux 子连接自行结束后才会被清理（约 2.7–13 分钟），期间该会话仍被持续 LIST 轮询。原因是 XDRIVE 既没有对端存活检测，也没有背压。

Version: v26.10.17 (`92ccc93`, the newest release and the same commit as current `main`), `network: "xdrive"`, `service: "local"`. XDRIVE is only in the pre-releases since v26.9.30; it is not in v26.3.27. The session logic involved does not depend on the backend, so remote backends behave the same way.

When an XDRIVE client disappears in the middle of a download (process killed, network lost, which is common for mobile clients), the server does not notice:

1. It keeps reading from the target and writes the whole remaining response into the storage. In the repro the client had received 22 MiB of a 256 MiB body; within 20 s after the client was killed the server wrote 246,869,084 bytes in 607 objects.
2. These objects stay until the server-side mux sub-connection ends on its own: about 2.7 min when the target closes the connection after the body, about 13 min with a keep-alive target. Meanwhile the dead session is still polled (about 2 LIST per second).
3. The server logs nothing after the client is gone, even at `debug`.

With a remote backend every abandoned download can upload hundreds of MiB into the storage account, consume API quota and leave the objects there for minutes.

If only the application connection is closed while the client stays alive (curl killed), the server stops writing within about 5 s and the folder is cleaned up, so the problem is specific to the peer disappearing.

| 256 MiB body at 16 MiB/s, `sessionTtlSeconds: 30` | storage at +30 s | +90 s | +180 s | server kept writing |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| download completes (control) | 0 B | 0 B | 0 B | no |
| client `kill -9` after ~2 s | 246,869,084 B / 607 objects | same | same | yes, the whole remaining body |
| client `SIGTERM` after ~2 s | 246,394,446 B / 515 objects | same | same | yes |
| curl killed, client alive | 0 B (one `.end`) | 0 B | 0 B | no, stopped within ~5 s |
| client `kill -9`, keep-alive target, watched 900 s | 246,453,796 B | same | same | yes; empty only at ~750–780 s |
| client `kill -9`, target sends `Connection: close` | 246,485,923 B | same | 0 B | yes; empty at ~165 s |

**Cause**

- `Listener.claim` marks the session active (`transport/internet/xdrive/xdrive.go:225`); the mark is removed only in the connection's `onClose` (`xdrive.go:234`). `collect()` skips active sessions (`xdrive.go:267-269`), so the folder of a dead session is not collected while the server-side connection is open.
- That connection is closed only when the inbound handler returns (`app/proxyman/inbound/worker.go:123-127`), i.e. after the server-side mux session ends. XDRIVE has no peer liveness signal: no heartbeat, no idle timeout. `Conn.receive` blocks on the reader channel (`conn.go:53-61`), `walReader.poll` returns quietly on an empty listing (`wal.go:295-297`), `holeTimeout` fires only when later segments exist (`wal.go:312-321`), EOF comes only from a `.end` object (`wal.go:365`).
- No backpressure: `walWriter.Write` appends to the buffer and `flushLocked` starts `go w.upload` (`wal.go:73-91`, `wal.go:127-156`); the semaphore in `upload` limits concurrent `Put`s, not unconsumed data (`wal.go:161-166`). Segments are deleted only by the peer's reader, so nothing limits what

issues.title: [Bug]: Xray-core VLESS+TUN 模式下 Moonlight 串流连接失败 (RTSP handshake failed: -1)
TLS: Fix data race between certificate hot reload and handshakes
issues.body:
in `transport/internet/tls/config.go` the ocsp callback had a block like this:
  ```go
  } else if string(newOCSPData) != string(cert.OCSPStaple) {
      cert.OCSPStaple = newOCSPData
  }
  ```
  `cert` here is the same `*tls.Certificate` that `GetCertificate` has already returned, so the staple was being changed while handshakes could be reading it. `OCSPStaple` is a slice, so this write is not
  atomic and a handshake can see the old pointer with the new length or vice versa. this can end up in a truncated staple or in a read past the end of the buffer. the window is very small and i haven't
  reproduced it on a real handshake

  now the callback makes a copy of the certificate, sets the new staple on the copy and publishes it, so a certificate that was already returned is never changed. to publish the copy safely
  `BuildCertificates` now returns `[]*atomic.Pointer[tls.Certificate]` instead of `[]*tls.Certificate`, it's only called from `GetTLSConfig`

  i have added a test with a local ocsp responder which checks that a previously returned certificate keeps its staple. it fails without this change even without `-race`

issues.title: GitHub Actions: Use Android packed relocations for Android builds
issues.body:
Android builds are PIE, and a Go PIE binary carries ~155k `R_*_RELATIVE` dynamic relocations (pointers in type descriptors, itabs, static string/slice headers, etc.). Stored as plain RELA (24 bytes each) they take **3.56 MiB** of every Android binary.

This PR passes `-Wl,--pack-dyn-relocs=android` to lld (NDK r28b, already used by the Android jobs), so the table is stored in Android's packed format (APS2) instead.

### Result (NDK r28b, same command line as `release.yml`)

| | before | after | diff |
|---|---|---|---|
| android-arm64-v8a | 36,447,032 B | 33,380,312 B | **−2.92 MiB (−8.4%)** |
| android-amd64 | 39,053,016 B | 35,980,920 B | **−2.93 MiB (−7.9%)** |
| relocation table (arm64) | 3,738,216 B (`RELA`) | 671,475 B (`ANDROID_RELA`) | |

The download (zip) shrinks less (~0.3 MiB) because RELA compresses well; the gain is mostly on-disk / installed size. Code and data are unchanged: only the encoding of the relocation table differs (e.g. `.data.rel.ro` has the same size in both builds).

### Compatibility

- `DT_ANDROID_RELA` is supported by the bionic loader since **Android 6.0 (API 23)**. The Android jobs already target API 24 (`*-linux-android24-clang`, "Android 7+" since #4664), so the supported range does not change.
- Binaries would fail to load on Android 5.x (API 21–22), which is already below the build target.
- RELR (`--pack-dyn-relocs=relr`) would save ~0.6 MiB more, but needs Android 9 (API 28, `DT_ANDROID_RELR`) or Android 11 (API 30, `DT_RELR`), so it is intentionally **not** used here.

### Testing

On a physical device (Android 16 / API 36, arm64), comparing the unchanged build with the packed one:

- `xray version`, `xray x25519`, `xray run -test`: OK
- end-to-end traffic inside the device: dokodemo-door → VLESS outbound → VLESS inbound → freedom → metrics HTTP endpoint: `200 OK`
- unit tests cross-compiled with the same flags and run on the device (`common/buf`, `common/crypto`, `common/protocol`, `common/serial`, `common/net`, `infra/conf`, `proxy/vless/encoding`, `app/router`): identical results for both builds, all PASS (geosite-dependent router tests skipped: no `geosite.dat` on the device)

Not tested on Android 6–8 hardware; compatibility there is based on the dynamic tags (`llvm-readelf -d` shows `ANDROID_RELA`/`ANDROID_RELASZ`) and bionic's documented support.

issues.title: REALITY: post-handshake records not imitated for empty SNI
issues.body:
### Integrity requirements

- [x] I have read all the comments in the issue template and ensured that this issue meet the requirements.
- [x] I confirm that I have read the documentation, understand the meaning of all the configuration items I wrote, and did not pile up seemingly useful options or default values.
- [x] I provided the complete config and logs, rather than just providing the truncated parts based on my own judgment.
- [x] I searched issues and did not find any similar issues.
- [x] The problem can be successfully reproduced in the latest Release

### Description

**Version:** Xray-core v26.10.21, the latest release. It bundles REALITY `83f6217`, which is the current REALITY `main`. v26.7.28 (REALITY `9234c77`) has the same code, and that's where I first noticed it. The `ServerName: sni` probe config involved has been in place since the per-SNI detection was added in REALITY `21af070` (June 2025).

### Summary

REALITY copies the target's post-handshake records (NewSessionTicket) for every name in `serverNames` except the empty one, `""`. For `""`, the startup probe `DetectPostHandshakeRecordsLens` fails before it sends anything, and the failure is silent. The key for empty SNI then gets `[]int{}`, so authenticated clients without SNI get no post-handshake records at all, even when the target sends them to a client without SNI.

This is the same mismatch [Aparecium](https://github.com/ban6cat6/aparecium) exploits (#4778), the one the post-handshake record imitation was added to fix. For connections without SNI, that fix has no effect, and Aparecium still detects them.

### Why this matters

No-SNI is a documented REALITY feature: see `serverName` in the [REALITY docs](https://xtls.github.io/en/config/transports/reality.html), which say "the server-side `serverNames` must contain an empty string `""`". It is also useful in practice right now. In Russia, connecting without SNI is one of the ways around the newer SNI-based restrictions, sometimes working better than ClientHello fragmentation, and it is easier to set up in many clients than fragmentation is. So it shouldn't be dismissed as a niche option. Users who turn it on fingerprint themselves without knowing it: they get weaker camouflage than the other names on the same inbound, with no warning. The fix is two lines, only touches the startup probe, and doesn't change behaviour for named entries.

### Cause

[`record_detect.go#L61`](https://github.com/XTLS/REALITY/blob/83f621788ca88b83179810b12baa7ae518aacb83/record_detect.go#L61) and [`#L96`](https://github.com/XTLS/REALITY/blob/83f621788ca88b83179810b12baa7ae518aacb83/record_detect.go#L96) both build the probe's config like this:

```go
uConn := utls.UClient(detectConn, &utls.Config{
	ServerName: sni, // "" for the empty entry
	NextProtos: nextProtos,
}, fingerprint)
```

uTLS refuses a ClientHello that has an empty `ServerName` while certificate verification is on ([`handshake_client.go#L53`](https://github.com/refraction-networking/utls/blob/aa6edf4b11af82e110eea845bb2983d30138d651/handshake_client.go#L53)):

```
tls: at least one of ServerName, InsecureSkipVerify or InsecureServerNameToVerify must be specified in the tls.Config
```

So `Handshake()` returns before anything is sent, and the deferred function ([`record_detect.go#L32`](https://github.com/XTLS/REALITY/blob/83f621788ca88b83179810b12baa7ae518aacb83/record_detect.go#L32)) stores `[]int{}` for `"<target>  0"`, `"<target>  1"` and `"<target>  2"`. To check the stored values directly, I called `reality.DetectPostHandshakeRecordsLens` from a small program and dumped `GlobalPostHandshakeRecordsLens` 15 s later.

issues.title: TUN inbound: Route each new UDP destination, keeping FullCone NAT within a route
issues.body:
The UDP FullCone table (#5509) is keyed by the source only, and only the first packet of a session is routed, so later destinations of that source reuse its outbound. As the TUN never sees a socket close, a port that the OS reuses before the session expires inherits the old route. For example, DNS on a port last used by a direct or blocked flow never reaches the DNS outbound, and a resolver that retries from the same port (mDNSResponder) keeps the stale session alive.

Now a new destination is routed once, with fake IPs judged by their domain and no DNS lookup made. It then joins its source's session for the same rule, or gets a session of its own. Destinations of one rule still share a session, so FullCone is kept within a rule, and a balancer picking another outbound doesn't split it. Routing runs off the goroutine that reads the tun. WireGuard and MASQUE servers are unchanged.

Checked on a real utun on macOS with the system resolver: DNS on a reused port is answered and destinations of one rule leave from one port, while on main the DNS goes nowhere and every destination leaves from the first one. A new destination costs about 2 µs more; established flows and throughput are unchanged.

AI disclosure: this PR was completed using Claude Opus 5.5.

#7174 bolted a second Lua mask onto header-custom, which was the wrong way around. One `lua` mask covers all of it now: it is both a `tcpMasks` and a `udpMasks` entry, and the script decides what it does by the hooks it defines.

-- `HandleHeader(stream, address, role)`, TCP: a free handshake before any traffic, with `stream:Write`, `stream:Read` and `stream:Sleep`. Return a string or an error and the connection is dropped
-- `HandleHeaderWrite(header, address, role)` and `HandleHeaderRead(packet, address, role)`, UDP: prefix every packet with a header, and strip it on the other side by returning its length, or `nil` to drop the packet
-- `HandleNoise(plan, address, role)` is the old noise hook, so `noise`'s `script` is gone (it has not been in a release yet)
-- `role` is `client` or `server`, so one file serves both ends
-- a hook the script does not define is not wrapped at all: a noise only script leaves TCP connections alone and never touches a packet
-- the module is `xray.finalmask` now, with `Random` and `RandomBetween`

```json
{
    "udpMasks": [{"type": "lua", "settings": {"script": "mask.lua", "reset": "30-60"}}]
}
```

Per call it takes at most 64 noise packets and 65535 bytes of noise, 1024 bytes of header, and 65535 bytes each way in a handshake. A packet hook gets 1s, a handshake 30s. A UDP header is one Lua call per packet, the benchmarks in the package cover its cost.

The static lists can follow later, the same script can already do what they do.

issues.title: XHTTP: packet-down in stream-down with downlink keep-alive
issues.body:
# XHTTP: packet-down in stream-down with downlink keep-alive

Follows RPRX's packet-down design in https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/6755#issuecomment-5720463978, which was written while closing the earlier downlink-resume attempt (#6755). That attempt was rejected because "restore connection" is too complex, with latency, ACK and so on. This one does not attempt connection restoration at all. No reconnection, no state machine, nothing to tune: each stream-down GET stays a single request; if the GET dies, the connection dies the ordinary way.

## Problem (from #4846)

CDNs kill a stream-down GET on body inactivity. This matters during uploads: with packet-up the uplink posts keep flowing, but the downlink proxy payload only arrives while the origin sends, so during a pure upload the GET idles and gets cut. Same story for any target that goes quiet for a while after responding.

## What this PR adds

When enabled on both ends, the stream-down response body is cut into packet-down frames with the five elements from the design comment:

- omittable session id excerpt: first 8 bytes of the session id, present on data and keep-alive frames (absent in stream-one where the session id is empty)
- omittable packet seq: uint64, counting data/keep-alive frames per stream-down GET
- mandatory type: data or padding
- mandatory length: uint16
- payload

Use today is the first one from the design comment: downlink keep-alive. While the downlink has been idle for a whole period, the server writes a padding frame (base62, in the spirit of tokenish x-padding) instead of staying silent. Everything the dispatcher sends rides in data frames, which is what lets the client tell padding apart from payload safely; the seq keeps the format ready for the future uses listed in the design comment (retransmission, multi-path-down) without another wire change.

h1, h2 and h3 are covered, since the framers sit on the body, not on a specific transport. stream-one gets the same treatment on its single response body. Browser dialer is out of scope for now: it has no place to read the response header that confirms the framing.

## Negotiation

Strictly opt-in and per request, so old servers are unaffected and nothing breaks behind middleboxes:

1. client config has packetDown: XHTTP stream requests not used as pure uplink (stream-down GET, stream-one request) carry X-Packet-Down: 1
2. server has packetDown configured and sees the marker: it answers with X-Packet-Down: 1 on the response, and frames; without the confirmed header the client never parses frames
3. any other combination: byte-identical wire format as today

## Config

```jsonc
"xhttpSettings": {
  "path": "/sh",
  "packetDown": {              // absent = disabled, as today
    "keepAlive": true,
    "keepAlivePeriod": "10-30",  // seconds; padded when inactive this long. defaults to 10-30
    "keepAliveLength": "24-64"   // padding size. defaults to 24-64
  }
}
```

Server side is the same block in the inbound; the server only honors the feature when the client asks.

## Not in this PR (deliberately)

- obfs of the frames (later, per the design comment)
- retransmission, multi-path-down, same-packet racing, ACK: the format carries seq and the session excerpt, but none of the machinery, exactly like packet-up carries seq today without using it
- nothing about #4846's larger downlink freeze problem (the 15-20 KB per TCP connection cut): this only discards the CDN idle timer, it does not split data across connections

## Tests

- packet_down_test.go: frame round trip (with/without excerpt, with/without seq), byte-stream shaped like a socket, splitting payloads larger than one frame, padding skipped, malformed frame rejected, keep-alive written when idle, keep-alive suppressed while active, config normalization
- splithttp_test.go: full listen/dial round trip with packet-down on both end (100 KiB), and the fallback case with the client setting present but the server without one
- infra/conf: JSON un

issues.body:
```markdown
Follow-up to #6487, covering the startup-padding part of #6732.

Adds an optional `padding` array to XMC settings with configurable direction per turn:

```json
{
  "padding": [
    {"length": "44", "direction": "c2s"},
    {"length": "64-128", "direction": "s2c"},
    {"length": "25", "direction": "c2s"},
    {"length": "32768-49152", "direction": "s2c"}
  ]
}
```

Each entry specifies a fixed length or inclusive range, plus direction (`"c2s"` for client-to-server or `"s2c"` for server-to-client; full names `"client-to-server"` and `"server-to-client"` are also accepted). Turns can be in any order and direction, including consecutive same-direction turns. Both endpoints need the same array. The first length includes Login Acknowledged's two bytes; invalid ranges and directions are rejected during config loading and connection setup.

Omitting the `padding` field entirely preserves the existing 26.1.2 preset. Custom turns have no intentional delays. Data framing, keep-alives, and mask ordering are unchanged. No new dependency or wire-format change.

This deliberately leaves profile registries, version negotiation, and ongoing traffic scheduling for separate discussion. In particular, existing length checks are not a configuration-fingerprint handshake and do not detect every endpoint mismatch; the documentation calls this out.

Tests cover range validation, direction validation, prefix and VarInt boundaries, default-preset preservation, and encrypted bidirectional round trips with single, odd, and even turn counts.

issues.title: Bound shutdown after termination signal
issues.body:
This change prevents Xray from waiting indefinitely during graceful shutdown after receiving SIGTERM or interrupt.

Previously, shutdown depended on the deferred server.Close() call returning. If any feature Close() path blocked, the process could stay alive while listeners or active connections continued operating. This made stale Xray processes difficult to detect, especially when another process could bind the same port.

Now Xray runs server.Close() explicitly after receiving a termination signal and waits up to 10 seconds. If shutdown does not complete in time, the process exits with code 1 so supervisors can treat it as a failed shutdown and avoid leaving a functional stale process behind.

This issue was most visible on mobile clients. Some apps, such as Telegram proxy-style traffic, may continue using an already-established path even when the VPN/client UI appears disabled. If the old Xray process remains alive during a stuck shutdown, those connections can continue transferring traffic and updating usage counters, making the node look stopped from the client side while traffic is still flowing server-side.

issues.title: TLS : tls spoofing
issues.body:
fix #5964

### RawPacket aka TLS Spoofing

So first lets talk about the idea,

when you connect to a xray server, the censors can see your TLS ClientHello, read the SNI, and figure out what you are doing and block :)

The RawPacket aka TLS spoofing fixes that by injecting a fake TLS ClientHello before the real one Hits.


The fake one carries like a decoy domain (ex. baidu.com) and then the real one carries your actual destination (ex. www.example.com).

A sensor that captures the first packet sees baidu.com and think that you are just browsing, and everything is okay with that, but in reality your connection goes through :)


It can be configured in the `finalmask.tcp` okay? and its only for client side.


### How everything works


When Xray dials a TCP connection and the first `Write()` happens (which also triggers the real TLS handshake) , our Raw Packet setup does the following.

1.builds a fake Tls ClientHello with whatever SNI you want or you have option to provide the raw bytes (b64).

2.Then we. wrap it in a raw TCP/ip packet.

3.Then deliberately we corrupt the TCP header using whatever method is selected okay?

4. Then we shoot it out via a raw socket

5. Then immediately let the real `Write()` go through normally


In short : two packets arrive at the server back to back and the fake one gets dropped by the servers TCP stack because of the corruption and then the real handshake proceeds like nothing happened.


### Config Example

```json
{
  "streamSettings": {
    "finalmask": {
      "tcp": [
        {
          "type": "rawpacket",
          "settings": {
            "sni": "baidu.com",
            "payload": "",
            "method": "wrong-sequence",
            "ttl": 3,
            "count": 1
          }
        }
      ]
    }
  }
}
```


### Available Fields

`sni` : The domain to put in the fake ClientHello. If you set this, it will auto generate a valid TLS ClientHello for you automatically. If you set `payload` and `sni` same time , sni wins here.

```
"sni": "baidu.com"
```

`payload` : If you don't want an auto gnrated ClientHello, then just encode your raw bytes that you want into base64 and put them here. I have added an option to do it from command line also. Do like this 

```
 xray tls fake-hello google.com
 ```

It will out the thing and then just copy paste.


Note : If `sni` and payload are empty or not set , the raw packet does nothing and the connection goes through normally.


`method` : It defines how we corrupt the fake packet so the server drops it.

`wrong-sequence` : It duplicates the sequence number (looks like a retransmission so server drops it)

So we grab the kernels `snd_nxt` ( the next sequence number the kernel expects to send), then subtract the length of the fake payload and then use that as the sequence number of the injected packet. The results then is a duplicate of the. last segment, so the receivers TCP stack sees it as a retransmit at best, or like out of window at worst and then drops it.


`wrong-checksum`: It flips all the bits in the TCP checksum (so server sees a bad checksum and drops it)

We build the packet with a correct checksum and then flip every bit(^0xFFFF). The receiver then validates the checksum and its wrong, so the packet goes in trash.

`wrong-ack`: It sets ACK number way outside the receive window (so server sends dup ACK then drops it)

It sets the ACK number to `rcv_nxt - window/2` and that's way outside of the receivers window, and the kernel responds with a dup ACK containing the correct sequence number, then drops it.

`wrong-md5` : This adds a fake TCP MD5 signature option and server without MD5 drops it

Here we append a TCP option with kind=19 and length=18 to the TCP header. The kind 19 is the MD5 signature option (RFC 2385), if the receiver doesn't use TCP MD5 (which is basically everything except some BGP routers), it sees an unknown option

issues.body:
## Summary

An XHTTP response write can hold the connection mutex while blocked on a slow reader. Closing the logical connection then waits on that mutex, including when a proxy inactivity timeout cancels the business context while the HTTP request stays open.

Signal closure before waiting for the writer and interrupt an active write using `http.ResponseController`. Serialize the complete transition with `sync.Once` so concurrent business/handler closes join the deadline call and the writer before `ServeHTTP` returns.

```text
Close (once)
  signal closure
  interrupt active write
  wait for writer completion
```

## Evidence

- Added `TestConcurrentCloseWaitsForDeadline`, using a real HTTP test server and a gated response writer. The gates ensure the business close owns the first deadline call before the handler closes.
- Upstream implementation: fails with `Close waited for the blocked writer without interrupting it`.
- An unserialized close transition: fails with `deadline call outlived ServeHTTP during concurrent Close`.
- Commit `8628110`, rebuilt with Go 1.27.3 on Linux/amd64: `go test -buildvcs=false ./transport/internet/splithttp -count=1` passes (`ok`, 2.434s).
- Bounded loopback `packet-up` fixtures run against a binary rebuilt from commit `8628110`: peer half-close and an internal inactivity timeout with the HTTP request still open both finish with `CLOSE_FRAMES=0`, `WRITE_FRAMES=0`, and `CLOSE_WAIT_CONNECTIONS=0`.

## Merge Danger

**Door:** Two-way.

**Blast Radius:** XHTTP shutdown. Active I/O is interrupted on close; the existing transport tests cover normal completion.

issues.title: XHTTP: Add configurable error responses
issues.body:
## What

Adds an optional `errorResponse` object to the XHTTP inbound settings, replacing the bare status-only rejections with a service-consistent appearance.

Currently every rejected request is answered with a bare status code: no body, no `Content-Type` (Go's default "404 page not found" or nothing at all). From the terminating side (CDN, reverse proxy, monitoring) a server that answers *every* unknown path with a naked status code and no content type does not look like a normal service.

- `body` and `contentType` apply to every error response the hub writes (404 unknown path, 400/405/409/413/500 etc.), giving all rejections a uniform, service-consistent appearance.
- `statusCode` overrides the status for requests failing the padding validation — the effective authentication gate — allowing 403 semantics instead of the default 400.
- When `errorResponse` is unset, the behavior is unchanged.

Example:

```json
"xhttpSettings": {
  "path": "/api/v2/stream",
  "errorResponse": {
    "statusCode": 403,
    "body": "{\"error\":\"forbidden\"}",
    "contentType": "application/json"
  }
}
```

Resulting surface: unknown paths → `404 {"error":"forbidden"}`, the API gate without valid padding → `403` with the same body — a coherent API host instead of a bare 404/400 machine.

## Notes

- Server-side only. Round-trips through `extra` like the other settings.
- `config.pb.go` regenerated with protoc v6.33.5 / protoc-gen-go v1.36.11 (matches all existing `.pb.go` headers; unmodified proto regenerates byte-identical with this toolchain).
- Proto field `errorResponse = 31` — merges cleanly alongside #7247 (`responseHeaders = 30`); both features are independent.

## Tests

- `Test_WriteErrorResponse`: bare default when unset, configured body + content type, padding-reject status default (400) and override (403).
- `go test ./...` passes locally across all packages, except the pre-existing network-dependent `TestQUICNameServer` in `app/dns`, which fails identically on pristine `main` in my environment (no QUIC egress).

issues.title: XHTTP: Add configurable response headers
issues.body:
## What

Adds an optional `responseHeaders` map (`map<string, string>`) to the XHTTP inbound settings, giving the server control over the headers it writes on responses.

Currently the hub hardcodes a set of response headers: the CORS block for the browser dialer (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials`, `Access-Control-Allow-Methods`, `Access-Control-Allow-Headers`), `X-Accel-Buffering`, `Cache-Control` and the SSE `Content-Type`. With `responseHeaders` an operator can add, override, or remove any of them, as well as set arbitrary extra response headers.

## Semantics

- A key that doesn't collide with a default header is added to every response.
- A key that matches a hardcoded header overrides it.
- An empty value removes that header from the response entirely (including the hardcoded ones).
- When `responseHeaders` is unset, the behavior is byte-identical to before.

Example:

```json
"xhttpSettings": {
  "path": "/api/v2/stream",
  "responseHeaders": {
    "Server": "nginx",
    "Cache-Control": "no-cache, no-transform",
    "Access-Control-Allow-Origin": "https://example.com",
    "X-Accel-Buffering": ""
  }
}
```

## Why

- The CORS headers only matter for the browser dialer; a plain server deployment currently emits `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on every response, which is undesirable behind a specific origin and gets flagged by security reviews.
- Reverse-proxy and CDN setups sometimes require specific response headers (`Server`, `Via`, custom headers) or different cache semantics.
- Operators running behind intermediaries may want the response header set to stay consistent with the profile of the service they front, instead of carrying markers that no other service on that endpoint emits.

## Notes

- Server-side only; the client ignores it. It round-trips through `extra` like the other settings.
- `config.pb.go` regenerated with protoc v6.33.5 / protoc-gen-go v1.36.11 — the header matches all existing `.pb.go` files (`check-proto` passes; I verified the unmodified proto regenerates byte-identical with this toolchain first).

## Tests

- `Test_SetResponseHeader`: default / override / removal via empty value.
- `Test_WriteResponseHeader_ResponseHeaders`: CORS default, override, removal, custom header addition, origin echo.
- `go test ./...` passes locally across all packages, except the pre-existing network-dependent `TestQUICNameServer` in `app/dns`, which fails identically on pristine `main` in my environment (no QUIC egress).

issues.title: grpc: close cached clients with their outbound handler
issues.body:
Related to #7177. Requesting review of resource ownership, shutdown semantics, and API compatibility

## Problem

Outbound gRPC clients are cached by destination and MemoryStreamConfig, but core shutdown never closes or removes them. In an embedding process that stays alive, clients can retain connections and continue reconnecting after their core has stopped.

## Change

Give memory stream settings synchronous close-hook registration, and close the resources from their owning outbound handler. Register each ClientConn for exact-entry cache removal and ClientConn.Close. Refuse both reuse and creation after owner closure starts; racing creation must either register for cleanup or close its unpublished client. Cleanup runs outside the settings/cache locks, and concurrent Close callers wait for the same result.

The supported Instance lifecycle is single-start. Each fresh core retains separate ownership even when endpoint and outbound tags match. No per-run generation model, idle-timeout change or per-RPC closure of the shared ClientConn is added.

## Validation

- Synthetic regression reproduces the problem on v26.3.27 and main da2248c.
- `go test -race ./transport/internet ./transport/internet/grpc -count=1 -timeout=120s` passes on this exact branch.
- Official `go run ./infra/vformat/main.go -mode check -pwd ./` passes.
- Tests cover two live cores, sibling streams, normal/MultiMode, fresh-core cycles, failed-start cleanup, multiple destinations, owner/acquisition races, cancellation/backoff and forced dialerProxy lookup contention with Manager.Close.
- Earlier candidate testing also ran the target race suites five times and the dialerProxy test ten times. Those results are supplementary, not a claim that the whole upstream suite passes.

## Review questions / limits

- Handler.Close previously always returned nil. This candidate propagates cleanup errors. Is propagation preferred, or should transport cleanup be logged while preserving the existing return policy? Embedders must distinguish a cleanup error from a still-running core.
- MemoryStreamConfig with resource/mutex state must not be copied; direct external transport callers must close their settings.
- Manager.RemoveHandler still bypasses Handler.Close. XHTTP/nested download settings and TUN eventfd cleanup remain unfixed.
- No general multi-instance guarantee for Xray's other process-global networking state, TLS/Reality/masking matrix, or physical Android packet boundary is claimed.

This is intended as a draft for ownership/API review, not a claim that the Android product defect is resolved.

Outbound: Close the handler when removing it; VLESS Reverse Proxy: Don't start after closing
issues.body:
`outbound.Manager.RemoveHandler`, which `xray api rmo` (`HandlerService.RemoveOutbound`) calls, deletes the handler from the map but never closes it, while `inbound.Manager.RemoveHandler` does. So whatever the removed outbound's `Close()` would release keeps running:

- WireGuard creates its TUN in the constructor (a kernel TUN when available, otherwise a gVisor stack), and once used also has the device with its UDP socket and keepalives.
- VLESS with `reverse` keeps its monitor task: the removed outbound keeps dialing the server every 2 s.
- Same for MASQUE's tunnel. VLESS with `testpre` gets closed too, but its pre-connects only stop reliably with #7113: on main, `Close()` stops just the goroutines waiting to hand over a connection, not the ones redialing an unreachable server.

This shows up wherever outbounds are added and removed at runtime through the API, e.g. by panels.

### Changes

- `RemoveHandler` closes the handler it removed. It does so after releasing the manager lock, so a slow `Close()` (WireGuard) doesn't hold up `Select()`/`GetHandler()` for new connections. Removing an unknown tag still returns nil, and a removed handler is closed only once, since `Manager.Close()` no longer sees it.
- VLESS starts the reverse 2 s after the outbound is created (a goroutine in `New()`), so an outbound removed within those 2 s would still start it after `Close()`. `Reverse.Start()` is now a no-op once `Reverse.Close()` has run.

The other callers of `RemoveHandler` (commander, metrics, reverse portal, VLESS inbound's reverse) remove their own internal outbounds, whose `Close()` is a no-op or idempotent.

Connections already in flight on a removed outbound behave as before unless its `Close()` tears them down (WireGuard, MASQUE). A reverse bridge that is already connected is left to end on its own; only new ones stop.

### Reproduction (on 836a6fe)

Client: `api` with `HandlerService` behind a dokodemo-door inbound, `freedom` as the only configured outbound. Server: a plain TCP listener that only counts accepted connections.

**VLESS `reverse`**: the outbound is added with `xray api ado` and removed with `xray api rmo`. Afterwards `xray api lso` lists only the `freedom` outbound in all runs.

| `rmo` after `ado` | build | accepts at `rmo` | 3 s later | 13 s later |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 7 s | main | 3 | 4 | 9 |
| 7 s | this PR | 3 | 3 | 3 |
| 0.5 s | main | 0 | 1 | 6 |
| 0.5 s | this PR | 0 | 0 | 0 |

**WireGuard** (`noKernelTun: true`): five outbounds, each added with `ado` and removed right away with `rmo`. Goroutines from the `metrics` listener's `/debug/pprof/goroutine`: main 11 → 72, this PR 11 → 12.

issues.title: XTLS Vision: Serialize VisionWriter writes from concurrent mux sessions
issues.body:
Fixes #7336

Since 4064f8dd the VLESS inbound hands its `VisionWriter` to `mux.Server.DispatchLink` without a pipe. `mux.ServerWorker` writes from one goroutine per session, so `VisionWriter.WriteMultiBuffer` runs concurrently. The padding state (`writeOnceUserUUID`, `IsPadding`, `NumberOfPacketToFilter`) changes outside any lock, while the `BufferedWriter` lock underneath only covers the socket write. Blocks then reach the wire in a different order from the one their padding was computed in. The client `VisionReader` passes padding through as data, and the client mux fails with `unknown status: <random>`, dropping every session on the connection. Details, configs and logs are in the issue.

This PR makes `VisionWriter.WriteMultiBuffer` hold its own mutex for the whole call, so the padding state and the wire order change together. Mux writes were already serialized by the `BufferedWriter` lock, so throughput stays the same. On plain TCP Vision only one goroutine writes, so the lock is never contended. The same change covers the VLESS reverse portal with Vision, where `mux.ClientWorker` writes from one goroutine per session.

`TestVisionWriterConcurrentWrites` writes to one `VisionWriter` from two goroutines while the underlying writer holds the first write until the second one lands. Without the lock the second block goes out first without the user UUID, and a `VisionReader` on the other side returns padding bytes as payload. The test is deterministic: it fails on `main` without the change and passes with it, with `-race` as well.

The repro from the issue (100 UDP associations at once through Vision + XUDP):

| | replies of 100 | server data races (`-race`) |
| -- | -- | -- |

Hysteria inbound: Reject duplicate `email`, fail on unknown one in `RemoveUser`
issues.body:
The Hysteria validator does not check emails:

- [`Add`](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/1c8bf4067b881e5f21442882013d0617e4d5dc6d/proxy/hysteria/account/config.go#L52-L62) stores a second user with an email that is already present.
- [`DelByEmail`](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/1c8bf4067b881e5f21442882013d0617e4d5dc6d/proxy/hysteria/account/config.go#L64-L77) then removes whichever of them `sync.Map` iterates first and returns nil, so the other password keeps authenticating after a successful `RemoveUser`. It also returns nil for an unknown email.

VLESS and Trojan reject both cases ([VLESS](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/1c8bf4067b881e5f21442882013d0617e4d5dc6d/proxy/vless/validator.go#L35-L59)). This makes the Hysteria validator do the same: emails are compared case-insensitively, `Add` rejects an existing email, `DelByEmail` fails on an empty or unknown one.

Before the fix, add `u@example.com` with `pass-A`, add it again with `pass-B` (both nil), `DelByEmail("u@example.com")` (nil): one password still authenticates, `GetCount` is 1.

Test: `proxy/hysteria/account/config_test.go` fails before the change and passes after; `go vet ./proxy/hysteria/...`.

> Short answer: yes — almost all of the extra write time is Google-side, not your line. Two separate Google effects are stacked on top of the 110–130 ms RTT
> 
> **1. Drive writes are synchronous backend commits, reads are cache hits.**
> A `GET` description/body is served from Drive's metadata/content caches, so it lands near RTT + small overhead (measured p50 ≈ 350 ms read vs ≈ 800 ms inline write on the same line at parallelism 1). A write (`PATCH` for inline, multipart upload for media) must transactionally commit metadata + content and update indexes before it returns 200 — that commit costs several hundred ms of *server* time regardless of how fast your line is. So inline write p50 ≈ RTT + ~450–650 ms commit; media ≈ upload + commit ≈ 1.7 s. The 1 KB-vs-14 KB PATCH delta was small, so it's not bandwidth — it's the commit path. Your 110–130 ms line only sets the floor; it can't remove Drive's commit time.
> 
> **2. Concurrent-write rate limiting (a real Google quota).**
> At parallelism 1 writes are ~0.8–1.7 s; at p=8/12 the same writes blow up to p50 ~3 s and p95 19–33 s, with `403 userRateLimitExceeded` and our cooldown/throttle counter climbing. That degradation is Drive throttling/queueing concurrent writes per user — a Google limit, not your line and not our code. It's why the write gate / parallelism sweep mattered: past the knee, adding parallelism *reduces* goodput.
> 
> So: reads ≈ your line; writes ≈ your line + Drive commit; parallel writes ≈ your line + Drive commit + Drive throttle. The earlier latency-floor decomposition (net floor vs GET vs PATCH) put the code's share as minor and the write commit at ~0.6 s.
>

Right, the TUN UDP table has no timeout of its own; a session only ends when its outbound goes idle.

A timeout has a limit here, though: it only removes a mapping that stops receiving packets. When the system resolver gets the port of a finished flow, its retries go to that stale mapping and keep it active. macOS mDNSResponder retries a stuck query from the same port at intervals shorter than the timeout, so the mapping never expires and the name stays unresolvable.

issues.title: [Feature Request][Windows] Add "Close to system tray" option
issues.body:
# [Feature Request][Windows] Add "Close to system tray" option to prevent accidental VPN disconnection

## Problem

On Windows, clicking the standard window close button (X) exits AmneziaVPN and disconnects the active VPN connection.

There is currently no option to make the application hide to the system tray instead of exiting.

The standard minimize button (-) only minimizes the application to the taskbar, leaving an unnecessary taskbar entry.

For a VPN client intended to run continuously in the background, this is inconvenient and potentially disruptive. Accidentally closing the window can immediately interrupt network connectivity.

## Proposed solution

Please add a configurable **"Close to system tray"** option:

- Clicking X hides the window to the system tray without terminating the application or disconnecting the VPN.
- The active VPN connection remains uninterrupted.
- Clicking the tray icon restores the main window.
- An explicit **Exit** command in the tray menu allows users to terminate the application intentionally.
- The standard minimize button (-) retains its normal Windows behavior.

Ideally, closing the window should not silently disconnect an active VPN connection.

## Environment

- OS: Windows 11 Home 26H2
- Build: 26300.9711
- Application: AmneziaVPN for Windows

## Why this matters

This is standard behavior for many applications designed to run continuously in the background.

VPN connectivity should not be interrupted merely because a user wants to dismiss the application window.

A simple setting would significantly improve usability and help prevent accidental disconnections.

issues.title: fix(macos): build a working installer without a signing identity
issues.body:
## Why

Building the macOS installer locally without an Apple Developer identity
failed or produced an app that did not start:

- `pkgbuild` crashed because CPack passed `--sign "" --keychain ""`;
- `macdeployqt` invalidates the signatures of the Qt frameworks and plugins,
  so on Apple Silicon the unsigned app was killed on start
  (`SIGKILL (Code Signature Invalid)` while loading `libqcocoa`).

## What changed

- `CPackOptions.cmake`: the productbuild/pkgbuild identity and keychain
  variables are set only when they are non-empty.
- `sign_binaries.cmake`, `codesign.cmake`: without `CODESIGN_SIGNATURE` the
  binaries are signed ad hoc (`--sign -`), without `--timestamp` and
  `--options runtime`, which require a real identity. Builds with an identity
  are unchanged.

## Testing

- macOS 27 (Apple Silicon), no signing identity: `deploy/build.sh` produced
  the `.pkg`; `codesign --verify --deep --strict` passes on the app; installed
  and ran.
- Not tested: a build with a real identity (the code path is unchanged).

issues.title: fix: connect to and manage servers over IPv6
issues.body:
## Why

Access providers block the IPv4 addresses of many VPS while their IPv6
addresses stay reachable. The client could not use them:

- `host:port` was split on every `:`, so an IPv6 address broke the SSH
  credentials input and WireGuard config import (#1037);
- the WireGuard/AmneziaWG server address was always sent to the daemon as
  IPv4, producing `endpoint=2001:db8::10:51820` in UAPI (also addressed by the
  open #3364; here the address goes to the IPv6 field, which the daemons
  already bracket);
- the macOS and Linux kill switch blocked all IPv6, including the server;
- exported native configs wrote `Endpoint = 2001:db8::10:51820`.

## What changed

- `NetworkUtilities::parseHostPort`, `endpointHost`, `endpoint`: one parser
  for `host`, `host:port`, `[IPv6]`, `[IPv6]:port` built on
  `QHostAddress`/`QUrl`; an unbracketed IPv6 is never split. Used by the SSH
  credentials input, `PayloadSender` and WireGuard import.
- WG/AWG transport: the server address goes to `serverIpv6AddrIn` or
  `serverIpv4AddrIn` by family; brackets in the wg-quick writer (Windows),
  `WGConfig.swift` (iOS) and the native export templates
  (`$SERVER_ENDPOINT_HOST`); Windows adapter lookup via `GetBestRoute2`.
- Kill switch: macOS `allownets` rule is `quick`; Linux `110.allowNets` is
  installed for both families before `250.blockIPv6` and fills `ip6tables`
  for IPv6 entries; the service validates IPv6/CIDR entries.
- macOS: `MacOSFirewall::uninstall` flushes every `amn/*` sub-anchor.
  Before, only the root anchor was flushed, sub-anchors kept the rules of the
  previously installed version, and `enableAnchor` never reloaded the updated
  files (it skips non-empty anchors). This affects any pf rule change on
  upgrade, not only IPv6.
- Tunnel ranges: IPv6 AllowedIPs ranges are sent with `isIpv6: true` (`/128`
  default for a bare host); `Address = v4, v6` is split into the device IPv4
  and IPv6 addresses.
- Tests: `test_host_port_parsing`, `test_wireguard_endpoint_import`.

## Testing

- macOS 27 (Apple Silicon), self-hosted dual-stack server: AmneziaWG
  connected with `Endpoint = [IPv6]:port` and IPv4 traffic in the tunnel, kill
  switch on; server added as `[IPv6]:port`, managed over SSH via IPv6 while
  connected, users added.
- `test_host_port_parsing` passes (43 cases).
- Not tested: Windows and Linux builds (the platform code was not compiled
  locally), Android and iOS builds, `test_wireguard_endpoint_import`, protocols
  other than AmneziaWG.

## Known limitations (not in this PR)

- XRay on desktop: `StopRoutingIpv6` cuts the connection to an IPv6 server.
- IPv6 inside the tunnel stays blocked by the kill switch on macOS/Linux.
- IPv6-only servers: server scripts and Docker networks are IPv4-only.
- `DNS =` with IPv6 servers in imported configs is not parsed.

issues.title: Deadlock between AmneziaVPN-service and kernel network locks on lid close (macOS 26.6, app 5.0.0.5, VLESS) — configd killed by WATCHDOG
issues.body:
## Summary

On macOS 26.6 (25G72), closing the MacBook lid while the VPN is connected reliably
deadlocks the system networking stack. A kernel lock cycle forms between
`AmneziaVPN-service` and the kernel, `configd`'s `IPConfigurationAgentQueue` stalls,
and after 60 seconds the watchdog terminates `configd`.

This happens every single day, on every lid close with the VPN running.

## Environment

- AmneziaVPN for macOS **5.0.0.5**
- macOS 26.6 (build 25G72)
- MacBookPro18,3 (Apple Silicon)
- Protocol: **VLESS (XRay)**
- `tun2socks` is present in the process list (41 threads), consistent with the
  XRay/VLESS userspace tunnel path
- Report incident ID: 19D61D4C-C90C-4BF8-AE79-91B9C65CAC96
- Report type: bug_type 409 (WATCHDOG stackshot), `displayState: OFF`

## Steps to reproduce

1. Connect the VPN.
2. Close the MacBook lid.
3. Within ~60 seconds a `configd` watchdog report is generated.

## Actual result

`configd` is killed by the [watchdog]

## Root cause from the stackshot — four-way lock cycle

1. `configd` thread 103010 (`IPConfigurationAgentQueue`) waits on kernel mutex
   `0xfffffe000c571830`, owned by kernel thread 103456 (`thread call high #27`).
2. Kernel thread 103456 waits on krwlock `0xfffffe000c5a4270` **for reading**,
   owned by thread 104354.
3. Thread 104354 belongs to **AmneziaVPN-service (pid 553)** and waits on kernel
   mutex `0x5162d882b476c1c1`, owned by kernel thread 5256.
4. Kernel thread 5256 waits on mutex `0xfffffe000c571830` — back to 103456.

The cycle never breaks, so the whole networking subsystem stalls.

## Additional observations

- `AmneziaVPN-service` had **259 threads** and **~955 MB** resident memory, with
  ~592k page faults. Roughly 200 of those threads were parked on the same
  `0xfffffe000c571830` mutex, and about a dozen more on the krwlock held by 104354.
  The thread and memory growth looks like a leak independent of the deadlock.
- `tun2socks` (41 threads) is blocked on the same mutex.
- The `AmneziaVPN` GUI process is also stuck: thread 16371 waits on krwlock
  `0xfffffe000c5a4270` for writing, owned by 104354.

## Likely trigger

On lid close macOS tears down Wi-Fi and reconfigures interfaces, so `configd`
dismantles network services while the client simultaneously tears down its `utun`.
The two sides appear to acquire the network locks in opposite order.

## Workaround

Disconnecting the VPN before closing the lid avoids the issue entirely.

## Attachment

issues.body:
## Description
Connecting via AmneziaWG (container `amnezia-awg2`) fails instantly: the UI shows 
"Connecting" for ~1 second, then drops back to "Disconnected". 
The daemon log shows a peer public key parsing error, after which the daemon 
crashes with a core dump and is restarted by systemd.

The same server/config works fine on other family members' devices (non-Linux), 
so the server side is OK.

## Environment
- OS: Linux Mint 22.3 (x86_64)
- Client versions tested: 5.1.0.6 (ac175c8) and 5.0.3.0 (de93650) — same bug on both
- Protocol: AmneziaWG (container `amnezia-awg2`)
- Connection route mode: VpnOnlyForwardSites (site split tunneling also tested disabled — same result)
- Daemon binary: /opt/AmneziaVPN/bin/AmneziaVPN-service (systemd unit AmneziaVPN.service)

## Steps to reproduce
1. Open AmneziaVPN
2. Select server with AmneziaWG protocol
3. Click Connect
4. Connection drops after ~1 second

## What was already tried (no effect)
- Reinstalled the client (5.1.0.6 → 5.0.3.0)
- Removed server profile and re-added it with a freshly issued config
- Disabled site split tunneling completely
- Wiped user config (~/.config/AmneziaVPN.ORG)
- Restarted AmneziaVPN.service, rebooted the PC multiple times

## Actual result
Interface `amn0` is created, `amneziawg-go` starts, but peer configuration fails:
AmneziaVPN WireguardUtilsLinux : Created wireguard interface amn0
AmneziaVPN LinuxRouteMonitor : Adding exclusion route for /999999
AmneziaVPN LinuxRouteMonitor : Invalid destination prefix
AmneziaVPN WireguardGo : ERROR: (amn0) IPC error -22: failed to get peer by public key:
hex string does not fit the slice
AmneziaVPN WireguardUtilsLinux : Peer configuration failed: Unknown error -22
AmneziaVPN Daemon : Peer creation failed.
AmneziaVPN DaemonLocalServerConnection : Failed to activate the interface
malloc(): unsorted double linked list corrupted
AmneziaVPN.service: Main process exited, code=dumped, status=6/ABRT
AmneziaVPN.service: Failed with result 'core-dump'.
Note also the garbled peer key in the daemon log 
(`Configuring peer Ϯ⇈C5 via <server IP>`) — looks like memory corruption 
while parsing the peer public key, which then leads to the malloc() crash.

## Expected result
AmneziaWG tunnel connects normally, as it does on other devices with the same server.

## Additional info
The issue is specific to AmneziaWG — the daemon crashes during peer setup, 
before any handshake, so this is not a network/provider block.

comments.issue_title: Deadlock between AmneziaVPN-service and kernel network locks on lid close (macOS 26.6, app 5.0.0.5, VLESS) — configd killed by WATCHDOG
comments.body:
Still happens on 5.1.0 build 6 (package 5.1.0.6). No sleep or lid close in my case: the last wake was about 12 hours before the panic, and I was using the machine at the time.

- AmneziaVPN 5.1.0 (6)
- macOS 26.5.2 (25F84), Mac16,13, 16 GB
- VLESS/XRay, tun2socks on utun22, KillSwitch on
- Docker Desktop was running, but its threads are not in the lock graph

The spindump report of the relaunched GUI shows the cycle:

```text
Deadlock: AmneziaVPN-service thread 0x3feee7 -> kernel_task thread 0x268 -> tun2socks thread 0x61c11b -> AmneziaVPN-service thread 0x3feee7
Blocked by Deadlock: 8 tasks
```

The same cycle in `waitInfo` of the configd watchdog stackshot:

| Thread | Holds | Waits on |
|---|---|---|
| AmneziaVPN-service 4189927 | mutex `0xfffffe000c5bff50` | krwlock `0xfffffe000c5f2830` (read), held by kernel_task 616 |
| kernel_task 616 | krwlock `0xfffffe000c5f2830` (write) | a mutex held by tun2socks 6406427 |
| tun2socks 6406427 | that mutex | mutex `0xfffffe000c5bff50`, held by AmneziaVPN-service 4189927 |

All three threads are `TH_WAIT, TH_UNINT`. 16 tasks are stuck behind them.

Some details:

- The service thread in the cycle runs Go code (`runtime.asmcgocall`) and is blocked in `write()` -> `sosend()`. I assume it's the in-process Xray core writing to its outbound socket. The middle of its kernel stack matches the tun2socks thread frame for frame.
- `…bff40` / `…bff50` are probably `pf_perim_lock` and `pf_lock`: an rwlock and a mutex 16 bytes apart, and all three stuck pfctl processes wait on `…bff40` for write inside `ioctl()`. The release kernel has no symbols for these frames, so this is a guess.
- configd (`IPConfigurationAgentQueue`), mDNSResponder, syslogd and apsd wait on `…bff40` for read, queued behind the pfctl writers.

Timeline (UTC):

```text
20:21:35  tun2socks starts, VLESS connected
20:36:21  pfctl #1 starts (parent: AmneziaVPN-service), never returns
20:36:28  last TCP event on utun22
20:36:42  I quit the app; client logs "Failed to disable killswitch", "Failed to restore resolvers", "Failed to delete tun"
20:36:54  GUI crashes with SIGSEGV (stack below)
20:37:21  pfctl #2 starts, parent: launchd
20:37:51  pfctl #3 starts, parent: bash
20:38:09  hang report of the relaunched GUI with the Deadlock line above
20:40:52  configd watchdog stackshot, IPConfigurationAgentQueue unresponsive
20:43:23  panic: userspace watchdog timeout: no successful checkins from configd (1 induced crashes) in 180 seconds
```

Telegram kept reconnecting through the tunnel the whole session: 1753 TCP connections in about 14.5 minutes, 1687 of them closed with 0 bytes received. So the "lots of sockets through the tunnel" trigger mentioned earlier in this thread fits here too, but as a steady load rather than a burst.

About the pfctl timeout mentioned earlier in this thread: `QProcess::waitForFinished()` defaults to 30 s ([docs](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qprocess.html#waitForFinished)). On timeout the `QProcess` in `MacOSFirewall::execute()` is destroyed and kills bash, while pfctl stays stuck and is reparented to launchd. That is pfctl #2 above. So each call is capped at about 30 s, but `XrayProtocol::stop()` runs them one after another. pfctl #1 was started by the service directly, without bash, so that path may have no cap at all.

None of this helps once the cycle has formed: the stuck processes can't be killed (as reported earlier in this thread), and the panic came about 7 minutes after the first stuck pfctl.

The GUI crash on quit is probably a separate bug (maybe related to #2931 / #3042):

```text
EXC_BAD_ACCESS (SIGSEGV), KERN_INVALID_ADDRESS at 0x0000000000239364
Thread 9 (QThread, crashed):
  QtCore
  VpnProtocol::connectionStateChanged(Vpn::ConnectionState)
  VpnProtocol::setConnectionState(Vpn::ConnectionState)
  XrayProtocol::stop()
  VpnConnection::disconnectFromVpn()
  QObject::event(QEvent*)
  ...
  QThread::exec()
Thread 0 (main):
  QThread::wait(QDeadlineTimer)
  AmneziaApplication::~AmneziaApplication()
